parts: Lesson 5: Impact of British Rule on India: Economic, Social and Cultural (1757–1857) — Summary

After Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India in 1498, the Portuguese, Dutch, French and English came to trade and to spread Christianity. Britain's Industrial Revolution needed raw materials and markets, and the decline of the Mughal Empire gave the British a chance to gain power through wars, forced treaties, annexations and alliances. Land revenue policies, commercial crops, monopoly of trade, railways and English education helped them establish and continue their rule.

The East India Company was set up in 1600. Its first factory was at Surat (1613); in 1615 Sir Thomas Roe got Jahangir's permission for factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach; Fort St. George was built at Madras; and in 1696 three villages in Bengal were developed into Calcutta (Kolkata) with Fort William.

The Battle of Plassey (1757), after which Mir Jafar was made Nawab of Bengal, and the Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) against Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and Shah Alam II, laid the base of British power. Mysore under Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan fought four wars; Tipu died in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799). The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19) ended Peshwa rule. After Maharaja Ranjit Singh's death, the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845, 1849) led Dalhousie to annex Punjab.

Under the Doctrine of Lapse, a protected state whose ruler died without a natural heir was annexed: Satara (1848), Sambalpur, Udaipur, Nagpur, Jhansi (1854) and Awadh (1856). Under the Subsidiary Alliance, Indian states disbanded their armies, kept British troops and gave up control of foreign affairs in return for protection.

In 1813 the Company's trade monopoly ended and India became an economic colony of industrial England. British machine-made cloth entered India duty-free while Indian goods were taxed heavily, so Indian handlooms collapsed (de-industrialisation): India changed from an exporter of cloth to an exporter of raw cotton and importer of British cloth, and weavers became farm labourers.

Land revenue: the Permanent Settlement (Lord Cornwallis, 1793, Bengal and Bihar) made zamindars hereditary owners who paid a fixed sum; if they failed, their land was sold. The new zamindars became allies of the British. The Mahalwari Settlement (1822; North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Ganga valley, parts of Central India) assessed a mahal (village or group of villages) jointly. The Ryotwari Settlement (Bombay and Madras) taxed the individual cultivator directly. All demanded very high revenue.

Commercialisation of agriculture: tea, coffee, indigo, opium, cotton, jute, sugarcane and oilseeds were grown for British needs. Farmers were forced to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land, which made the soil infertile. Food production fell and famines followed. Peasants borrowed from moneylenders, who used false accounts and high interest, and their land passed to the money-lending class. A new middle class of agents, new zamindars and English-educated professionals arose. Wealth was drained to Britain.

Railways connected raw-material areas with ports; British investors got a guaranteed 5% profit and free land. The first railway was the Red Hill line in Madras (1837, for granite); the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane (1853). Dalhousie opened the first telegraph line (Calcutta–Agra) and postal service. Railways also, unintentionally, brought people and ideas together.

Practices such as sati, child marriage, female infanticide and untouchability were common. Western ideas of liberty and equality inspired reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan. Laws: sati banned (1829, Lord Bentinck); Widow Remarriage Act (1856); inter-caste marriages allowed (1872); Sharda Act (1929) against child marriage.

Education policy: English was taught to create cheap, loyal clerks and a market for British goods. The Charter Act of 1813 gave Rs 1 lakh for education; Wood's Despatch (1854) led to Departments of Education and universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). Mass education was ignored, but English became the link language, spread ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism (Locke, Mill, Rousseau; Mazzini and Garibaldi became heroes). Orientalists set up the Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings, 1781), the Asiatic Society of Bengal (William Jones, 1784), the Sanskrit College at Banaras (Jonathan Duncan, 1794) and Fort William College (Wellesley, 1800).
Administration and courts: Indians were kept out of high posts; codified laws and civil and criminal courts were introduced, but justice was costly and discriminated between Europeans and Indians.

Heavy taxes, eviction and frequent famines led to revolts of Sanyasis and Fakirs, Poligars, Mappilas, Jats, Kolis, Bhils and Santhals. The Revolt of 1857 united people of different backgrounds, ended Company rule and gave rise to nationalism; afterwards the British followed a policy of Divide and Rule. Railways, English language, civil services, clothes and food habits remain as legacies of British rule.
